essential: Tuppence is accosted in St. James's Park by a big, clean-shaven, heavy-jowled man with small shifty eyes. He says he overheard her in Lyons' and followed her. She instinctively distrusts him but is unafraid.
His card reads Mr. Edward Whittington, Esthonia Glassware Co., with an eleven o'clock appointment the next morning. Keep her terrier-like shake and the 'adventures have begun' resolve.
She wires Tommy, using his retained pencil: 'Don't put in advertisement. Will explain to-morrow.' Keep the ninepence-versus-five-shillings economy.
At the office a middle-aged clerk at a desk in the small outer office shows her through a 'Private' door. Keep the outer office's existence and the clerk's ordinariness.

The offer: £100 down plus expenses for about three months at Madame Colombier's pensionnat in Paris, as Whittington's ward. Conditions are no communication with friends and absolute secrecy. He suggests she pass as an American because of her accent.

She objects that the terms are too liberal. He says he is paying for intelligence, presence of mind and discretion not to ask questions. She insists the deal is 'both or neither' with her partner Beresford.

Asked her name, she blurts 'Jane Finn' to spare the archdeacon. Do NOT explain here where the name came from; Ch. III reveals that Tommy mentioned it. Whittington's face turns purple with rage and dismay.

Tuppence bluffs by telling literal truths: Rita knows nothing of her; she knows 'very little'; it might be her own name or chance. Each answer deepens his unease. Keep the double-bluff logic and his 'How much do you know? And how much do you want?'
She proposes 'a little something down' and denies blackmail ('payment of services in advance'). Whittington shows grudging admiration.
The clerk brings a 'telephone message'. Whittington frowns, dismisses him as Brown, abruptly gives her £50 and tells her to return tomorrow. Do not hint that the clerk matters.
Whittington becomes suspiciously genial again, which gives Tuppence a faint misgiving. She leaves elated and takes a taxi to surprise Tommy.

Her walk to the end of the street to avoid looking over-eager, and taking the stairs rather than the lift, can be cut.

The au revoir exchange can be shortened, but keep his 'clever and charming young lady' and her misgiving.

continuity_checks: The clerk is called Brown only once, in Whittington's dismissal, with no narrative emphasis.
The 'Jane Finn' name is not explained as coming from Tommy.
Rita is mentioned by Whittington, not Tuppence.
The amount handed over is fifty (£), in notes that include five-pound notes, consistent with the taxi line.
The wire text is preserved so Ch. III's 'You're not going to put that thing in after all?' makes sense.
Tommy's pencil is retained by Tuppence.
risks: The haggling dialogue is the comic core. Over-trimming it may lose the escalating truth-as-bluff logic, so keep at least three of her truthful replies.
title: MR. WHITTINGTON’S OFFER
voice_profile: Brisk, comic third-person narration in close focus on one young adventurer at a time. It works through quick dialogue tags ('snarled', 'sweetly', 'moralized'), slangy period banter ('old bean', 'keep her end up', 'a dirty trick!'), and wry narrative asides that undercut the heroics: Tuppence admiring her own ingenuity, or Tommy reasoning 'in his usual slow and steady way'. Suspense comes from short paragraphs, dashes, trailing ellipses and abrupt chapter-end cliffhangers. Characters are often 'telling the truth' in ways others misread. Menace is conveyed through physical tells such as shifty eyes, purpling faces and a sibilant voice, and through ironic political epigram.
book_context: A 1920s thriller built on the joint venture of Tommy and Tuppence. Chapters alternate between their separate adventures and end on cliffhangers. Recurring mechanisms include accidental truth-telling that works as a bluff; names dropped casually that become clues ('Jane Finn', 'Rita', the clerk 'Brown'); and the faceless 'Mr. Brown', always suspected to be an unnoticed person present in the room. The approaching date of the 29th drives the plot. Chapter II plants the clues that Carter and Tuppence later decode in IV and VI. Chapter VIII plants the date, the conspirators' faces, Jane's mysterious incapacity and the recess hiding-place, all of which pay off in XVI, XVII and the climax in XXVI–XXVII. Abridgment must keep these plants without explaining them early.
